WAGE STATEMENT ITEMIZATION POLICY
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

POLICY STATEMENT
Acme, Inc. maintains this Wage Statement Itemization Policy to describe how Acme, Inc. prepares and furnishes itemized wage statements to Jordan Lee and other employees with each payment of wages. This policy describes the categories of information a wage statement includes, how deductions are itemized, and how Jordan Lee may request to inspect or obtain a copy of records pertaining to Jordan Lee's employment. This policy is a statement of Acme, Inc.'s practice; it does not itself create, waive, expand, or limit any right or obligation that may exist under applicable law.

THE NINE REQUIRED ITEMIZED STATEMENT ITEMS
California law requires Acme, Inc. to furnish Jordan Lee an accurate itemized wage statement, in writing, at the time of each payment of wages (or semimonthly), showing: (1) gross wages earned; (2) total hours worked by Jordan Lee, except as separately provided for certain exempt or salaried categories; (3) the number of piece-rate units earned and any applicable piece rate, if Jordan Lee is paid on a piece-rate basis; (4) all deductions; (5) net wages earned; (6) the inclusive dates of the pay period; (7) Jordan Lee's name and only the last four digits of Jordan Lee's social security number, or an employee identification number other than a social security number; (8) the name and address of the legal entity that employs Jordan Lee; and (9) all applicable hourly rates in effect during the pay period and the corresponding number of hours worked by Jordan Lee at each hourly rate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) An employer, semimonthly or at the time of each payment of wages, shall furnish to their employee, either as a detachable part of the check, draft, or voucher paying the employee's wages, or separately if wages are paid by personal check or cash, an accurate itemized statement in writing showing (1) gross wages earned, (2) total hours worked by the employee, except as provided in subdivision (j), (3) the number of piece-rate units earned and any applicable piece rate if the employee is paid on a piece-rate basis, (4) all deductions, provided that all deductions made on written orders of the employee may be aggregated and shown as one item, (5) net wages earned, (6) the inclusive dates of the period for which the employee is paid, (7) the name of the employee and only the last four digits of their social security number or an employee identification number other than a social security number, (8) the name and address of the legal entity that is the employer and, if the employer is a farm labor contractor, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1682, the name and address of the legal entity that secured the services of the employer, and (9) all applicable hourly rates in effect during the pay period and the corresponding number of hours worked at each hourly rate by the employee and, beginning July 1, 2013, if the employer is a temporary services employer as defined in Section 201.3, the rate of pay and the total hours worked for each temporary services assignment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226, subd. (a)) — used as evidence of the actual nine-item list California law requires on an itemized wage statement, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship. California's itemized-wage-statement requirement is unusually detailed and penalty-backed compared to many other states, some of which impose no itemized pay-stub requirement at all. Two of the nine items carry built-in statutory exceptions this list does not itemize in full: item (2) (total hours worked) is not required on the statement for certain salaried-exempt and other categories of employees the statute separately defines, and item (8) requires disclosure of an additional legal entity's name and address when the employer is a farm labor contractor. Item (9)'s temporary-services-assignment component applies only where the employer is a temporary services employer as separately defined, beginning July 1, 2013. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 226(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE ITEMIZED-DEDUCTIONS REQUIREMENT
California law requires that deductions from Jordan Lee's wages be itemized on the wage statement Acme, Inc. provides, not stated only as a single combined total. The one recognized exception is narrow: deductions Acme, Inc. makes on Jordan Lee's own written order may be aggregated and shown as one item. Acme, Inc. records deductions in ink or other indelible form, dated by month, day, and year, and retains a copy of each wage statement together with the deduction record for at least three years, at the place of employment or at a central location within California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(4) all deductions, provided that all deductions made on written orders of the employee may be aggregated and shown as one item,"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (a) (item 4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  "The deductions made from payment of wages shall be recorded in ink or other indelible form, properly dated, showing the month, day, and year, and a copy of the statement and the record of the deductions shall be kept on file by the employer for at least three years at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California. For purposes of this subdivision, "copy" includes a duplicate of the itemized statement provided to an employee or a computer-generated record that accurately shows all of the information required by this subdivision."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (a) (recordkeeping) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226, subd. (a)) — used as evidence of how California law treats wage-statement deductions, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's deduction practices. The statute's aggregation exception is narrow: only deductions made on the employee's own written order may be shown as a single combined item; the statutory text does not, on its face, authorize showing all deductions generally as one lump-sum figure. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subdivision (§ 226(a)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

SAMPLE WAGE STATEMENT ITEMIZATION
Each wage statement Acme, Inc. furnishes to Jordan Lee with a payment of wages is expected to show, at minimum: Jordan Lee's gross wages earned; Jordan Lee's total hours worked for the pay period (unless Jordan Lee's position is exempt from this item under applicable law); if Jordan Lee is paid on a piece-rate basis, the number of piece-rate units earned and the applicable piece rate; each deduction from Jordan Lee's wages, itemized separately, except that a deduction made on Jordan Lee's own written order may be shown as one aggregated item; Jordan Lee's net wages earned; the inclusive dates of the pay period; Jordan Lee's name and only the last four digits of Jordan Lee's social security number, or an employee identification number; the name and address of the legal entity employing Jordan Lee; and all applicable hourly rates in effect during the pay period, with the corresponding number of hours Jordan Lee worked at each rate. This description is illustrative of the categories a wage statement covers; the wage statement itself, not this policy, is Jordan Lee's official pay record.

THE STATUTORY PENALTY FOR A KNOWING AND INTENTIONAL VIOLATION
If Acme, Inc.'s failure to comply with the itemized wage statement requirements is knowing and intentional, and Jordan Lee suffers injury as a result, California law entitles Jordan Lee to recover the greater of all actual damages or $50 for the initial pay period in which a violation occurs, and $100 per employee for each violation in a subsequent pay period, up to an aggregate penalty of $4,000, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. An isolated and unintentional payroll error due to a clerical or inadvertent mistake does not, by itself, make a violation "knowing and intentional."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(e) (1) An employee suffering injury as a result of a knowing and intentional failure by an employer to comply with subdivision (a) is entitled to recover the greater of all actual damages or fifty dollars ($50) for the initial pay period in which a violation occurs and one hundred dollars ($100) per employee for each violation in a subsequent pay period, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of four thousand dollars ($4,000), and is entitled to an award of costs and reasonable attorney's fees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(e)(1), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (e)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  "(3) For purposes of this subdivision, a "knowing and intentional failure" does not include an isolated and unintentional payroll error due to a clerical or inadvertent mistake. In reviewing for compliance with this section, the factfinder may consider as a relevant factor whether the employer, prior to an alleged violation, has adopted and is in compliance with a set of policies, procedures, and practices that fully comply with this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(e)(3), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (e)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226, subd. (e)) — used as evidence of California's specific statutory penalty scheme for wage-statement violations, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This kind of automatic, per-pay-period statutory penalty for a pay-stub defect is unusually detailed compared to most other states, many of which provide no comparable private statutory penalty for wage-statement noncompliance at all. The $4,000 aggregate cap and the $50/$100 figures are the amounts the statutory text itself states; whether a particular failure is "knowing and intentional" is a fact question the statute does not fully define beyond excluding isolated, unintentional clerical or payroll errors, and the statute separately allows a factfinder to consider an employer's pre-violation compliance policies as a relevant factor. This is a distinct statutory right of action under § 226(e) itself; how it interacts procedurally with a civil penalty pursued under the Private Attorneys General Act (a related clause in this set covers that separately) is not addressed by the quoted text and is not asserted here. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 226) — subdivisions (e)(1) and (e)(3) — rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

WHAT COUNTS AS "SUFFERING INJURY" UNDER THE PENALTY PROVISION
For purposes of the knowing-and-intentional penalty, California law deems Jordan Lee to suffer injury if Acme, Inc. fails to provide a wage statement at all, or if Acme, Inc. fails to provide accurate and complete information for one or more of the nine required items and Jordan Lee cannot promptly and easily determine, from the wage statement alone: the gross or net wages paid; the other item (2)-(4), (6), or (9) information; which deductions were made; the name and address of the employer; or Jordan Lee's name and last four SSN digits or employee ID number. "Promptly and easily determine" means a reasonable person would be able to readily ascertain the information without reference to other documents or information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(2) (A) An employee is deemed to suffer injury for purposes of this subdivision if the employer fails to provide a wage statement. (B) An employee is deemed to suffer injury for purposes of this subdivision if the employer fails to provide accurate and complete information as required by any one or more of items (1) to (9), inclusive, of subdivision (a) and the employee cannot promptly and easily determine from the wage statement alone one or more of the following: (i) The amount of the gross wages or net wages paid to the employee during the pay period or any of the other information required to be provided on the itemized wage statement pursuant to items (2) to (4), inclusive, (6), and (9) of subdivision (a). (ii) Which deductions the employer made from gross wages to determine the net wages paid to the employee during the pay period. Nothing in this subdivision alters the ability of the employer to aggregate deductions consistent with the requirements of item (4) of subdivision (a). (iii) The name and address of the employer and, if the employer is a farm labor contractor, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1682, the name and address of the legal entity that secured the services of the employer during the pay period. (iv) The name of the employee and only the last four digits of their social security number or an employee identification number other than a social security number. (C) For purposes of this paragraph, "promptly and easily determine" means a reasonable person would be able to readily ascertain the information without reference to other documents or information."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(e)(2)(A)-(C), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (e)(2)(A)-(C) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226, subd. (e)(2)) — used as evidence of California's specific statutory test for when an employee is deemed to suffer injury for purposes of the knowing-and-intentional penalty, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This is a single, continuous statutory paragraph (§ 226(e)(2)(A)-(C)); no additional independent source was sought for this specific test. Most states with any wage-statement requirement do not define an injury threshold this specifically; California's definition is notably detailed, distinguishing a complete failure to provide a statement from a statement that omits or obscures particular required items.

THE RIGHT TO INSPECT AND COPY EMPLOYMENT RECORDS
California law gives Jordan Lee, as a current or former employee, the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to Jordan Lee's employment that Acme, Inc. is required to keep under the itemized wage statement requirement, upon reasonable request to Acme, Inc. Acme, Inc. may take reasonable steps to verify Jordan Lee's identity, and may charge the actual cost of reproduction for copies it provides. Acme, Inc. must comply with a request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request; failing to permit inspection or copying within that time exposes Acme, Inc. to a $750 penalty payable to Jordan Lee or the Labor Commissioner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) An employer that is required by this code or any regulation adopted pursuant to this code to keep the information required by subdivision (a) shall afford current and former employees the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to their employment, upon reasonable request to the employer. The employer may take reasonable steps to ensure the identity of a current or former employee. If the employer provides copies of the records, the actual cost of reproduction may be charged to the current or former employee. (c) An employer who receives a written or oral request to inspect or receive a copy of records pursuant to subdivision (b) pertaining to a current or former employee shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. A violation of this subdivision is an infraction. Impossibility of performance, not caused by or a result of a violation of law, shall be an affirmative defense for an employer in any action alleging a violation of this subdivision. An employer may designate the person to whom a request under this subdivision will be made."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(b)-(c), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subds. (b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  "(f) A failure by an employer to permit a current or former employee to inspect or receive a copy of records within the time set forth in subdivision (c) entitles the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner to recover a seven-hundred-fifty-dollar ($750) penalty from the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(f), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226, subds. (b), (c), (f)) — used as evidence of California's specific inspection-and-copy right and its enforcement deadline, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's recordkeeping. The 21-calendar-day compliance deadline, the $750 penalty for missing it, and the recognized "impossibility of performance" affirmative defense are all as stated in the quoted text; the statute also separately makes a violation of the 21-day deadline an infraction, which is a distinct consequence from the $750 penalty rather than a substitute for it. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 226) — subdivisions (b)-(c) and (f) — rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

PAGA EXPOSURE FOR WAGE STATEMENT VIOLATIONS
Beyond the private penalty described above, a wage-statement violation under California Labor Code § 226(a) may also be pursued through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee under the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA), Labor Code § 2699, on behalf of that employee and other current or former employees. PAGA gives an aggrieved employee an alternative avenue to recover, through a civil action, civil penalties that the Labor and Workforce Development Agency would otherwise assess and collect. For a PAGA claim based on the § 226(a)(8) item (the employer's name and address), the statute treats the violation as cured only if Acme, Inc. provides written notice of the correct information to each aggrieved employee, identifying the correct information for each pay period in which the violation occurred. For a PAGA claim based on a violation of § 226(a) items (1) through (7) or (9), the statute treats the violation as cured only if Acme, Inc. provides, at no cost, a fully compliant itemized wage statement (or, where that information is customarily provided digitally, reasonable access to a digital or computer-generated record containing the same information) to each aggrieved employee for each pay period in which the violation occurred during the three years before the notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "2699. (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any provision of this code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, for a violation of this code, may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of the employee and other current or former employees against whom a violation of the same provision was committed pursuant to the procedures specified in Section 2699.3."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.)
  "(2) (A) A violation of paragraph (8) of subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall be considered cured only upon a showing that the employer has provided written notice of the correct information to each aggrieved employee. Such notice may be provided in summary form but shall identify correct information for each pay period in which a violation occurred. (B) A violation of paragraphs (1) to (7), inclusive, and (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall be considered cured only upon a showing that the employer has provided, at no cost to the employee, a fully compliant, itemized wage statement or, if such information is customarily provided in digital form, reasonable access to a digital or computer-generated record or records maintained in the ordinary course of business containing the same information required on a fully compliant, itemized wage statement, to each aggrieved employee for each pay period during which the violation occurred during the three years prior to the date of the notice. Nothing in this subdivision will impact any right the employee has to request copies of employment records pursuant to Sections 226, 432, and 1198.5."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699(d)(2)(A)-(B), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699, subd. (d)(2)(A)-(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 2699) — used as evidence of how California's Private Attorneys General Act treats wage-statement violations specifically, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. PAGA itself is a distinctly Californian enforcement mechanism; most states have no comparable statute letting an employee sue for civil penalties that a state labor agency would otherwise be the one to assess and collect. This clause is deliberately narrow: it covers only the cure mechanism specific to a § 226(a) violation, not PAGA's general procedural requirements — the pre-suit notice process, the definition of "aggrieved employee," the default civil-penalty schedule under § 2699(f), or the allocation of any recovery between the state and employees — none of which are detailed here. No PAGA-related clause was found elsewhere in this document set to cross-reference (checked against the current clause library); if one is added later, this clause should point to it rather than duplicate its content. Whether a § 226(e) penalty and a PAGA civil penalty for the same wage-statement violation can both be pursued for the same conduct, or how they interact, is not addressed by the quoted text and is not asserted here. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 2699) — subdivisions (a) and (d)(2)(A)-(B) — rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

EMPLOYEE ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed a copy of this Wage Statement Itemization Policy. Jordan Lee understands that Jordan Lee may request to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to Jordan Lee's employment by directing a request to Acme, Inc., and that Jordan Lee may raise any question about the accuracy or completeness of a wage statement with Acme, Inc.

citations.quote: (b) An employer that is required by this code or any regulation adopted pursuant to this code to keep the information required by subdivision (a) shall afford current and former employees the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to their employment, upon reasonable request to the employer. The employer may take reasonable steps to ensure the identity of a current or former employee. If the employer provides copies of the records, the actual cost of reproduction may be charged to the current or former employee. (c) An employer who receives a written or oral request to inspect or receive a copy of records pursuant to subdivision (b) pertaining to a current or former employee shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. A violation of this subdivision is an infraction. Impossibility of performance, not caused by or a result of a violation of law, shall be an affirmative defense for an employer in any action alleging a violation of this subdivision. An employer may designate the person to whom a request under this subdivision will be made.

(f) A failure by an employer to permit a current or former employee to inspect or receive a copy of records within the time set forth in subdivision (c) entitles the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner to recover a seven-hundred-fifty-dollar ($750) penalty from the employer.

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the private penalty described above, a wage-statement violation under California Labor Code § 226(a) may also be pursued through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee under the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA), Labor Code § 2699, on behalf of that employee and other current or former employees. PAGA gives an aggrieved employee an alternative avenue to recover, through a civil action, civil penalties that the Labor and Workforce Development Agency would otherwise assess and collect. For a PAGA claim based on the § 226(a)(8) item (the employer's name and address), the statute treats the violation as cured only if Acme, Inc. provides written notice of the correct information to each aggrieved employee, identifying the correct information for each pay period in which the violation occurred. For a PAGA claim based on a violation of § 226(a) items (1) through (7) or (9), the statute treats the violation as cured only if Acme, Inc. provides, at no cost, a fully compliant itemized wage statement (or, where that information is customarily provided digitally, reasonable access to a digital or computer-generated record containing the same information) to each aggrieved employee for each pay period in which the violation occurred during the three years before the notice.

citations.quote: 2699. (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any provision of this code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, for a violation of this code, may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of the employee and other current or former employees against whom a violation of the same provision was committed pursuant to the procedures specified in Section 2699.3.

(2) (A) A violation of paragraph (8) of subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall be considered cured only upon a showing that the employer has provided written notice of the correct information to each aggrieved employee. Such notice may be provided in summary form but shall identify correct information for each pay period in which a violation occurred. (B) A violation of paragraphs (1) to (7), inclusive, and (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall be considered cured only upon a showing that the employer has provided, at no cost to the employee, a fully compliant, itemized wage statement or, if such information is customarily provided in digital form, reasonable access to a digital or computer-generated record or records maintained in the ordinary course of business containing the same information required on a fully compliant, itemized wage statement, to each aggrieved employee for each pay period during which the violation occurred during the three years prior to the date of the notice. Nothing in this subdivision will impact any right the employee has to request copies of employment records pursuant to Sections 226, 432, and 1198.5.
